messages.subject_clean: loess curves
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

A few weeks ago I asked for assistance on taking a set of time data, generating a smoothed curve for that data, and then calculating the rate of change of that time data. Kyle Gorman and Steve Piantadosi assisted me greatly by giving tips on how to use the loess() function and the diff() function. I've finally had time to go work through it and have attached my solution here in case it's of interest to anyone else. If I've made any conceptual (or other) errors, I very much welcome feedback on that. My data isn't actually some value over time, but a set of time values over steps.

The short version of my code is in the text of this email. I've also attached a pdf with the more extensive code and plots to see the results.

Hunter

---

In this data set, I have a set of Times over 51 steps. This data is divided into two conditions, low attachment (la) and high attachment (ha). I want to examine the time course of moving through these 51 steps in each condition. The shape of the main dataframe agg.rc.r.hala is
Centre		Time		Cond
1		62.927		la
2		61.441		la
3		67.678		la
4		64.070		la
5		66.825		la
I was interested in the rate of change between these values. However, I did not want the change on the raw data, but upon a smoothed curve. With suggestions from Steve Piantadosi and Kyle Gorman, I was able to get this using loess() for smoothing and then diff() for calculating differences between steps in the curve. You can do this directly on the Time data; however, that would have the rate of change increasing when the time was longer, while we typically think of velocity and acceleration as decreasing when the time is longer. So, the Times were inverted for further analysis. The inverse of the Time is giving the proportion of one step convered in 1ms. Here’s the basic code:
agg.rc.r.hala$InverseT <- 1/ agg.rc.r.hala$Time
#get the loess curve from the loess() function
rc.all.inv.la.lo <- loess(InverseT ~ Centre, agg.rc.r.hala[agg.rc.r.hala$Cond == "la",])
rc.all.inv.ha.lo <- loess(InverseT ~ Centre, agg.rc.r.hala[agg.rc.r.hala$Cond == "ha",])
#the result are the fitted values rc.all.la.lo$f
#use diff() function to calculate differences between values on the loess curve
#velocity
rc.all.inv.la.lo.v <- diff(rc.all.inv.la.lo$f)
rc.all.inv.ha.lo.v <- diff(rc.all.inv.ha.lo$f)
#acceleration
rc.all.inv.la.lo.a <- diff(rc.all.inv.la.lo.v)
rc.all.inv.ha.lo.a <- diff(rc.all.inv.ha.lo.v)

messages.subject_clean: lmer: main effects & interactions for a 4x3x2 design
messages.body_plain:
Dear R-langers,

This is a question about how to summarize a 4x3x2 mixed effects logistic
regression such that readers' eyes won't just glaze over.

What I've got is essentially the same experiment run 8 times (bear with
me). The experiment has three conditions. To make sure that arbitrary
aspects of the experimental design weren't responsible for any effects, I
varied one experimental parameter 4 ways and another one 2 ways. Hence
4x3x2.

This makes for a very long table if I want to list all the fixed effects.
Which I don't really want to do anyway, since they are mostly
uninteresting. I have around 1000 subjects, so understand that it wouldn't
be too bad to do model comparison. I think understand how to do that for
looking at the omnibus interaction:

model1 <-
lmer(response~(condition+nuisance1+nuisance2)^3+(1+condition|subject),data=mydata,family="binomial")
model2 <-
lmer(response~(condition+nuisance1+nuisance2)^2+(1+condition|subject),data=mydata,family="binomial")
anova(model1,model2)

[my stimuli are randomly generated and most are not repeated across
participants, so there's no reason to treat item as a random effect, so far
as I can tell]

but I'm less sure how to test other effects -- in particular, my main
effect. One option I looked at was

model3 <-
lmer(response~(nuisance1+nuisance2)^2+(1+condition|subject),data=mydata,family="binomial")
anova(model1,model3)

I get a result out (it's significant!), but I'm not sure if that's truly
testing a main effect or testing a main effect plus interactions. I tried

model4 <-
lmer(response~nuisance1+nuisance2+nuisance1:nuisance2+nuisance1:condition+nuisance2:condition+nuisance1:nuisance2:condition+(1+condition|subject),data=mydata,family="binomial")

but although that didn't list fixed effects of condition, it nonetheless
had the same dfs and same log likelihood as model1, so I'm not convinced
it's actually a different model. This may reflect my poor understanding of
how lmer actually works.

What is the right way to proceed? Alternatively, is there another way of
getting simpler, ANOVA-like summaries of the results?

Josh

Another vote for using data.table. Speed ranking (from slow to really fast) should be

aggregate > ddply > data.table

I'm using Mike's method, too. It might look a bit cryptic, but it's very, very fast! I guess this should be an issue for you, especially with over 2m rows in your original data.frame.

Maybe, you want to put an na.rm = T into the mean()-function. The may Mike wrote it up, you would get all NAs if one value is NA. Also, you might want to exclude the quotes around "year" after the by. So the call I would suggest should look like this:

> dSummary <- d[,list(cru_mean_ppt = mean(cru_mean_ppt, na.rm = T), udel_mean_ppt = mean(udel_mean_ppt, na.rm = T)),by=year]

If you want dSummary to be a data.frame again, just do an
dSummary <- as.data.frame(dSummary)
after finishing.

Sascha W.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Josh,

To get something along the line of an ANOVA table you could use mixed from afex which will test all fixed factors in your experiment using for example likelihood ratio test (which might seem indicated, given your rather large n).

require(afex)
model1 <- mixed(response~(condition+nuisance1+nuisance2)^3+(1+condition|subject),data=mydata,family="binomial", method = "LRT")

What afex does it that it subtracts the factors one by one and compares each model in which the factor of interest is removed against the full model (i.e., providing something similar to type 3 tests in the ANOVA framework).
When using method = "LRT" it makes the comparison using likelihood ratio tests (i.e., simply using anova on the two models), alternatively one can use method = "PB" in which case it will compare the two models using parametric bootstrap as implemented in PBmodcomp (package pbkrtest). However, then one will probably need a lot of time with 1000 subjects and need to set the number of samples to reasonable high values, e.g. with 1000 samples:

model1 <- mixed(response~(condition+nuisance1+nuisance2)^3+(1+condition|subject),data=mydata,family="binomial", args.test = list(nsim = 1000), method = "PB")

Note that a both of functionalities, fitting and obtaining bootstrap samples, can be parallelized using a snow cluster (via package parallel).


Finally, I have one more general comment. As I am relatively new to this list I would be really interested to hear what others think of the idea to test parameters by simply subtracting them from the model. Are there any obvious issues with this approach to test for the significance of factors?

Cheers,
Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

It is me again. I have a puzzling finding concerning the selection of 
random effect structure in LME. I did a time perception experiment in 
which participants reproduced the duration they had perceived. For the 
data analysis, originally, I used model comparisons to determine the 
random effect structure and chose the following model for my data.

Formula: RT ~ cStimulus * cDuration + (cStimulus + cDuration + 1 | Subject)
    Data: E1Flme

Fixed effects:
                       Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)         1745.35256   63.44293  27.511
cStimulus           -518.89263   94.11508  -5.513
cDuration              0.64573    0.05514  11.712
cStimulus:cDuration   -0.07019    0.03404  -2.062

As you can see, the results are quite expected; in particular, 
participants time reproduction is a function of the stimulus duration.

Later, following Barr et al (2013), I used a full random effect 
structure model:

Formula: RT ~ cStimulus * cDuration + (cStimulus * cDuration + 1 | Subject)
    Data: E1Flme

Fixed effects:
                       Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)         1745.35256   62.64032  27.863
cStimulus           -518.89263   72.68527  -7.139
cDuration              0.64573   46.34611   0.014
cStimulus:cDuration   -0.07019    2.19309  -0.032

Now,  the results are very different from the first model (e.g., no 
effect of duration, which is strange!). The lack of the duration effect 
seems to be due to the *huge* SE associated with the effect. The size of 
the SE is really incomprehensible given the size of the fixed effect 
there. Note that in the first model, the SE is reasonably small!

I attach the data here if anyone wants to have a try. I think this 
example illustrates the weird world of LME for beginners like me.

Zhenguang Cai

--

University of Plymouth

Thanks for a great discussion, all!  I hadn't updated yet, so I hadn't yet
experienced this.

I tried it out and replicated the problem you saw with v1.0-4

But it turns out that if you standardize Duration (not just center it), you
get pretty comparable results to the older lme4.  And if you just divide
Duration by 1000, again, more comparable results (though still somewhat
variable). It seems like even the old lme4 would sometimes have problems
converging when predictors had radically different scales.  So maybe these
issues get reflected in a different way in the new version.  I suspect that
transforming predictors to be on roughly similar scale is generally a good
practice for getting stable estimates for all versions of lme4, even if
that means you need to back-transform the resulting coefs for
interpretation.

Also, I'll just point out that there is very little data per subject.  So
maybe things would be a little less dependent on judicious transformations
if there was more data.  Just a speculation.

Code and results pasted in below.

best,
-scott

Hi Francesco,

As a first pass, would it make sense to recode the "s" and "of" responses
as "correct" and "incorrect" recall, or something like that?  So if they
correctly recalled "s" for an "s" or "of" for an "of", they get a 1, and if
they recall the "wrong" one, they get a 0.  You would then be looking to
see whether the rate of "correct recall" differs by what the correct recall
would be. In other words, is the probability of "correct" responses for "s"
greater than the "correct" responses for "of"?  So numerically, it looks
like 's is more correctly recalled than of.  If you re-code in this way,
you should get a pretty straightforward test of that.

If you think this makes sense for your data, for Question 2, it would just
be a matter of adding a native/non-native factor and seeing whether that
interacts with the "s/of" factor.  This would tell whether that the effect
of whether the target is 's/of on the probability of a correct response is
different for natives vs. non-natives.

That's my take on how I understand your data/questions.  The fact that you
have two other responses complicates things somewhat, but you could leave
those in unchanged, I think.

Are these counts the total for all subjects?  If so, there is a very low
occurrence of mismatches, with only four total cases of someone saying "of"
when they should have said "s".  As we've seen on this list, this can wreak
havoc on logit mixed models, especially if several of these are in just one
person.  So please proceed with caution!  In the end, you may,
unfortunately, find you need more data for lmer to give you sensible
results.

good luck!
-scott

Yes, lmer is pretty robust to uneven cell sizes, so you should worry about
it, unless some of your cells are extremely small, like I mentioned before.
 But you say that the counts in the full data are more, so maybe you're
safe there.  Just to be a little safer, I'd recommend summarizing the
counts for each subject, and see how many people have 0 counts in a
particular cell.  If there are lots, this may be a sign to be cautious when
fitting and interpreting your models.

When you say "I can't do this in R", I'm not sure what "this" refers to, so
I'm not sure how to help.  Depending on how you fit your models, and how
your factors/contrasts are coded, you may be able to get the contrasts
you're interested in from just the lmer model-fitting results.  I've
recommended the multcomp package a few times now on this list, but that may
or may not be helpful here.  If you try to use that package, it's important
to remember that it does two things: (1) provide an interface to get an
arbitrary (i.e., user-defined) set of contrasts from just one model-fit,
and (2) perform a correction on p-values to account for multiple
comparisons.  Whether you want to employ (2) depends on your attitude about
how you want to address the issue of multiple comparisons.  If you want a
large number of contrasts, (1) might be useful.  But to be honest, it
sounds like your design is not that complicated, so using multcomp might be
more work than it's worth.

Anyway, if you can be more specific about where you're getting stuck, I may
be able to give you more specific advice.
-scott
